themes.theme: Routes to market and central commercial agreements
themes.definition: Pre-arranged buying routes (frameworks, dynamic purchasing systems, memoranda of understanding, innovation routes) through which public bodies contract with AI suppliers, and the central support that comes with them (refines the starting code 'supplier contracts').
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 presents the Crown Commercial Service (CCS) as help across the whole buying process (existing guidance, routes to market, specifying requirements, running the procurement). It lists CCS frameworks and dynamic purchasing systems (DPSs) for buying AI, and notes memoranda of understanding with suppliers that give 'preferential pricing and discounts' through any route. It says CCS runs 'thorough ongoing supplier compliance checks' on frameworks so buyers have less to do at call-off, whereas on DPSs CCS does only basic checks and the buyer completes them at call-off (coder note); G-Cloud is excluded. UK136 names an overlapping set (G-Cloud, Digital Outcomes and Specialists, the Spark DPS, Innovation Partnerships, the GovTech Catalyst and the CCS AI DPS) and adds one substantive feature: specialist AI frameworks 'prescribe the terms and conditions' of later contracts and let buyers assess suppliers against predefined criteria 'that can include ethical requirements'. UK174 places the supplier-checking burden mainly on CCS, while UK136 presents supplier assessment as something the buyer is enabled to do; neither says what the criteria are. No route is required: they are 'useful starting points to consider' or routes to 'explore'.
themes.holders: Crown Commercial Service (UK174, UK136); CCS together with suppliers for the memoranda of understanding (UK174); GovTech Catalyst (UK136); holder not stated for UK136's list of framework agreements.
themes.binding: Not binding. All are offers or suggestions ('can guide you through', 'offers', 'useful starting points to consider', 'Explore'). No consequence is stated for not using them. The only duty-like element is the buyer completing supplier checks at call-off on DPSs (coder note on UK-COO-RES-007), stated as a description, not an obligation.
themes.checks: Only checks on suppliers, not on AI tools or their outputs. CCS supplier compliance checks (UK-COO-RES-007): trigger ongoing for frameworks, basic checks for DPSs with the buyer completing them at call-off; compared against not stated; metric or threshold not stated; who: CCS, and the buyer for DPSs; result: 'buyers have less to do at call-off'. Supplier assessment under specialist AI frameworks (UK-COO-RES-061): trigger at supplier selection [inference]; compared against 'a set of predefined criteria that can include ethical requirements'; metric or threshold not stated; who: the buyer; what happens with the result not stated.

themes.theme: Contract templates, clauses and supplier requirement checklists
themes.definition: Standard contracts, contract clauses and requirement checklists that set what suppliers must provide or guarantee, and the help available to draft them (refines the starting codes 'supplier contracts' and 'shared templates').
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 points buyers to a 'Data ethics requirements checklist for suppliers', which it says will mitigate bias and ensure diverse development teams, transparency, interpretability and 'explainability of the results', and to the Public Sector Contract, whose provisions cover intellectual property, data protection, and equality, diversity and human rights; neither passage names who issues these documents. UK174 also says the organisation's own lawyers will help draw up contracts and licences for AI tools. AI_Insights, on AI coding assistants, relies on what suppliers already offer: most enterprise or professional offerings 'include IP indemnity clauses', so the protection comes from the supplier's standard terms rather than a government template. UK136 adds that specialist AI frameworks pre-set the terms and conditions of any later contract. None of these passages specifies contract terms on access for testing, model versions, accuracy or performance levels, or notice of changes to the tool.
themes.holders: Not stated for the checklist or the Public Sector Contract (UK174); the organisation's lawyers (UK174); AI coding assistant suppliers offering enterprise or professional products (AI_Insights); Crown Commercial Service (UK136).
themes.binding: Not binding. Templates are provided or mentioned; the surrounding UK174 text (coder note) says it is 'important to consider and factor data ethics into your commercial approach from the outset', which is advisory. IP indemnity depends on the supplier's own offer ('Most ... include'). No consequence is stated.
themes.checks: No check on a tool or its outputs. The checklist names bias and 'explainability of the results' as supplier requirements, but trigger, what results are compared against, metric or threshold, who verifies, and what happens with the result are all not stated.

themes.theme: Information flowing between suppliers, model providers and public buyers
themes.definition: Instruments and channels through which a public body learns from suppliers or model providers what an AI tool is, how it works, what its limits are, or what is needed to take it over.
themes.what_is_set_out: Several documents give buyers ways to get information out of the supply chain, each narrow in purpose. UK174 points to PPN 02/24, which 'provides optional questions' to identify whether suppliers use AI in bids and in delivering services to government. UK099 points to the Responsible Handover Framework 'to identify the information needed' when an AI system passes from supplier to buyer, and UK071 recommends Explainability Matrices or AI Assurance Artefacts 'to clarify what is required from suppliers', without saying who supplies those artefacts. UK086 advises that, where a supplier is reluctant on intellectual-property grounds, the body walk it through the transparency-record questions and explain that they give only a high-level picture of the tool. In the other direction, AI_Insights says vendors 'frequently provide updates on well-known vulnerabilities', and UK139 lists CMA guidance that developers, deployers and end users 'need to be informed of the limitations' of foundation models. The purposes differ (procurement transparency, handover, assurance, publication, security, competition), and no passage places a duty on suppliers to disclose model versions, configuration changes or performance results.
themes.holders: Issuer of PPN 02/24 not named in the passage (UK174); Responsible Handover Framework, provider not named in UK-COO-RES-024 (the holder field of UK-COO-RES-025 attributes it to the Local Government Association) (UK099); teams in projects involving procurement or external suppliers (UK071); GDS as issuer of the advice (UK086); vendors and the data science community (AI_Insights); Competition and Markets Authority (UK139).
themes.binding: Weak. The PPN questions are 'optional' (UK174); UK071 is a recommendation ('Use', coded as 'teams should'); UK086 says 'it can help'; the vendor updates and CMA guidance are mentions. No consequence is stated if suppliers do not provide the information.
themes.checks: These are inputs to checks rather than checks. Vendor vulnerability updates (UK-COO-RES-039), which serve monitoring (coder note): trigger ongoing ('frequently'); compared against 'well-known vulnerabilities'; metric or threshold not stated; who: vendors and the data science community supply the information, the deploying body acts on it [inference]; what happens with the result not stated. Explainability Matrices or AI Assurance Artefacts (UK-COO-RES-029): trigger at planning and procurement (location 'Planning an…'); compared against not stated; metric not stated; who supplies them not stated; use not stated. Information on foundation model limitations (UK-COO-RES-050): trigger, comparison, metric, who and use not stated.

themes.theme: In-house commercial, legal and supplier-facing expertise
themes.definition: Staff inside the public body, chiefly commercial colleagues and lawyers, and the skills the documents expect to be available for dealing with suppliers and procurement rules (refines the Resources starting codes 'roles and staff' and 'skills and training').
themes.what_is_set_out: UK174 says commercial colleagues 'will be able to assist' with complying with procurement legislation, and that 'your lawyers will help you draw up the contracts and other agreements' for buying or licensing AI tools. AI_Insights describes commercial colleagues as holding knowledge of commercial processes, information assurance and data protection impact assessments, which developers adopting AI coding assistants should draw on; the DPIA appears only as a process they know about, not as a duty (coder note). UK266 treats the matter as a gap rather than a given: 'It is important for the government to have someone with the skills' to engage suppliers and 'cut through the hype', against an imbalance with often US-based technology providers (coder note). So UK174 and AI_Insights assume this expertise already exists in each body, while UK266 treats it as something government still needs to secure [inference]. No passage says how such staff are funded, trained or assigned to AI work.
themes.holders: Commercial colleagues (UK174, AI_Insights); the organisation's lawyers, 'your lawyers' (UK174); 'the government' (UK266).
themes.binding: Not binding. Stated as availability ('will be able to assist', 'will help', 'will have knowledge') or good practice ('It is important'). Nothing follows if the expertise is missing.

themes.theme: Pointers to other official guidance and toolkits
themes.definition: Cross-references in which one document directs readers to another document, toolkit or body of guidance instead of providing the support itself.
themes.what_is_set_out: Much of what is 'provided' in this cell is a pointer to another document. Procurement dominates: UK174 points to the Guidelines for AI procurement (and, per the coder note, the Sourcing Playbook and Rose Book Annex D), UK216 notes that 'the Office for AI has produced guidelines for procuring AI' and points to the EHRC's own procurement guidance for England, UK099 sends readers to the AI Playbook 'for further guidance on procuring AI systems', and UK136 describes the Office for AI's co-creation, with the World Economic Forum, of 'AI Procurement in a Box', a toolkit for procurement professionals 'across the globe'. Outside procurement, UK133 points to Government Social Research guidance on ethical assurance for its ethics review step, and UK099 to the Alan Turing Institute's stakeholder engagement overview. The procurement guidelines cited in UK174 and UK216 appear to be UK136 itself [inference], so several documents route readers back to the same older guidance. A pointer gives no access route, contact or support beyond the reference (coder note on UK-COO-RES-021).
themes.holders: Mostly not named in the passage; Office for AI (UK216; UK136, with the World Economic Forum Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution); Equality and Human Rights Commission (UK216); Government Social Research (UK133); Alan Turing Institute and Connected by Data (UK099); the UK Government AI Playbook (UK099).
themes.binding: Not binding. Pointers only ('For more information, read', 'For further guidance, please see', 'refer to'). No consequence.
themes.checks: n/a. The UK133 pointer serves an ethics review consultation step (coder note); its trigger, comparison, metric, who and result are not stated in this passage.

themes.what_is_set_out: UK133 suggests that consultation with key stakeholders 'could occur through workshops', possibly including pre-mortem sessions in which participants assume the intervention has failed (coder note). UK099 points to the Alan Turing Institute's stakeholder engagement overview for understanding stakeholders (and to Connected by Data, per the holder field). AI_Insights, in its guidance on using AI to manage shared drives, suggests giving business or asset owners 'an AI generated summary of the drives to help inform their assessment' before disposal, and says tooling can help 'conduct, control and record' that consultation. This last pair is the one place in the cell where an AI output is handed to a person to inform a decision, and the passages say nothing about checking the summary's accuracy or completeness before it is relied on.

absences: Coordination starting codes with no passages at all: notifications (no duty or channel to tell any body about a tool's use, a change to it, an incident or a failure) and referrals between bodies (there are only internal directories and suggestions to 'consult'; no formal route by which one body passes a case or a tool to another). Registers and databases appear only as the ATRS record template and contact address and as a proposed AI Knowledge Hub; no register of tools is provided as a resource in these passages. Resources starting codes that are thin: training (UK266 names a skills need, but no passage offers training); money (only Government Office for Technology Transfer funding for government-wide solutions and CCS pricing discounts, and nothing to fund coordination roles such as the ATRS lead or SPOC); time (only AI_Insights' 'allow yourself time'); data and access (no provision for sharing data or test sets, or for access to supplier systems for testing). A reader would also expect, and does not find: contract terms or shared templates obliging suppliers to disclose model versions, prompts or configuration, to give notice of changes, or to allow testing and audit; any channel for sharing evaluation results, error rates or incidents between bodies (the proposed Knowledge Hub's 'results' come nearest); named convenors, funding or terms of reference for the cross-government communities; and any stated scope or service level for the contact mailboxes.
cross_cutting: Procurement and supplier relationships are the largest concentration in this cell: routes to market, contract templates, supplier checklists, in-house commercial and legal help, and cross-references to procurement guidance, drawn mainly from UK174 and UK136. Around that sits a thin layer of central contact mailboxes, voluntary cross-government communities, a few hubs and shared frameworks, and the ATRS package, which is the only place where specific roles (a lead and a SPOC) are tied to a specific coordination task. Almost nothing is binding: resources are offered, pointed to or recommended ('can', 'consider', 'optional', 'could'), and no passage says what happens if a body does not use them or a provider does not deliver; the only roles asked of public bodies are the recommended ATRS lead and the SPOC described as already assigned in mandatory scope. Holders are mainly central units (CCS, DSIT teams, GDS, the Office for AI, the CDEI, the Government Office for Technology Transfer), regulators (Ofgem and the health regulators), and non-state or mixed providers (the Alan Turing Institute, BSI, NPL, the World Economic Forum, vendors); many passages, especially those on templates and communities, name no holder at all. On checking AI outputs the cell is close to silent. What it offers are inputs to checks (vendor vulnerability updates, information on foundation model limitations, supplier assurance artefacts, a checklist that names explainability of results, and UK071's statement of purpose as a shared testing reference), plus one case where an AI-generated summary informs a human decision with no stated verification. Nothing here coordinates the sharing of model versions, prompts, configuration, accuracy or consistency results, confidence scores or incidents, whether between public bodies or with suppliers. Documents also name different bodies or addresses for the same function (two AI assurance mailboxes; GDS as ATRS issuer with a DSIT contact address), and the passages do not reconcile them.
